blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled computer-using agents (CUAs) to
navigate the digital world through software interfaces ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ) . Given a natural-language instruction, an agent
observes the interface, plans, and acts, leaving a trajectory of thoughts,
actions, and observations. Digital tasks span applications in which success
can depend on visual presentation, application records, or changes to
persisted files. A trajectory can appear successful even when edits remain
unsaved or an operation fails without a visible warning. The agent may also
report completion after fulfilling only part of the instruction. Accepting
such a run as successful produces a false positive, making the distinction
between attempted actions and their actual effects central to verification.
Developing these agents therefore requires reliable judgments throughout
evaluation, data curation ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , and reinforcement
learning ( Xue et al., 2026a ) , including applications for which no
task-specific checker has been supplied.

blocks.en:
An execution can be verified online from the resulting machine state or
offline from its retained trajectory. Evidence can come from rendered
interfaces, structured observations, or artifacts such as files and database
records. VLM judges assess trajectories from selected
observations ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , while automatically generated checkers
inspect application state through model-written
programs ( Xue et al., 2026b ) . A fixed set of frames may
omit a decisive effect, and a generated query may target state that does not
answer the verification question. Platform-native signals support more
specialized judgments and validation ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026b ) , but their availability varies with the application and
access setting. Agentic approaches actively inspect trajectories or
environments ( Wan et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Sanayei et al., 2026 ) .
A shared procedure must seek relevant evidence under these access constraints
and ground its conclusions in the observations.

blocks.en:
To address these evidence and access limitations, we present VeriCUA, a
platform-agnostic framework that formulates CUA verification as agentic exploration (Figure 1 ). It provides a shared
procedure for offline and online verification using the sources and inspection
tools available in each setting. Verification begins after the executing
agent’s attempt ends. The verifier first explores the available context to
understand the app and its task artifacts, then uses these
observations with the instruction to construct a rubric of fine-grained
requirements. This context helps interpret task concepts and locate potential
evidence, especially when the application is unfamiliar. The verifier chooses
GUI or code tools to check the rubric’s requirements. Findings from these
checks reveal what remains unresolved and guide further inspection of relevant
frames, artifacts, or another available source.

blocks.en:
VeriCUA’s unified design separates the verification workflow from the
interfaces through which evidence is obtained. Offline verification navigates
retained screen frames and action logs, using structured observations such as
accessibility trees when recorded. Online verification can inspect the
accessible machine state left by the executing agent through GUI or code
tools, including files, databases, and system services. These sources answer
different questions about the requested outcome. An action log records an
attempted edit, while a file read can show whether the edited content
persisted. A report that the task is complete remains a claim to verify. The
framework links findings to their supporting observations and records source
properties such as frame timing or state persistence. Explicit evidence rules
combine the findings into a task verdict while retaining which requirements
are supported, refuted, or unresolved.

blocks.en:
We evaluate this shared procedure in offline and online scenarios on multiple
platforms. VeriCUA achieves higher agreement with reference labels than the
compared baselines in both settings. It also rejects more false completion
claims than the VLM judge in the online study. The action-space study shows
that adding code-based state reads enables more decisions without increasing
false positives. At a matched number of verification passes, adding visual
evidence improves agreement and decision coverage compared with repeating the
same configuration.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Computer-using agents are evaluated on web, mobile, and desktop
tasks ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Rawles et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) , with dedicated environments
covering scientific applications ( Sun et al., 2026c ) . These
benchmarks typically use task-specific programmatic evaluators to check
the resulting application state. Human-labeled trajectory datasets provide
reference judgments across applications ( Sun et al., 2026a ) , while
audits of benchmark evaluators identify errors in the checks used to
produce reference labels ( Xie et al., 2025 ) . Benchmarks of
environment-aware judges assess evidence acquisition and verification of
states and execution processes ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . Completion judgments
also support data curation and training beyond benchmark evaluation.
Trajectory synthesis pipelines use verifier scores to select
examples ( Sun et al., 2025 ) , and continual reinforcement learning
relies on automated feedback during environment
adaptation ( Xue et al., 2026a ) . Rubric-based reward modeling further uses
synthetic criteria derived from preferred and rejected
responses ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Safety-oriented evaluation additionally
examines whether agent behavior satisfies workflow
constraints ( Sun et al., 2026b ) . The range of applications and
evaluation criteria creates demand for verification that can locate
relevant evidence through available interfaces, including tasks without a
dedicated evaluator.

blocks.en:
VLM judges assess task completion from trajectory
observations ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , while structured critics evaluate
task requirements or intermediate milestones ( Li et al., 2026 ) .
Task-adaptive rubrics can be generated from task descriptions to guide
trajectory evaluation ( Ding, 2026 ) .
Generated verifiers construct programs that inspect application
state ( Xue et al., 2026b ) . Reward benchmarks evaluate
the reliability of trajectory judgments against reference labels across tasks and
platforms ( Sun et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . Agent-based
evaluators assess intermediate task requirements in code-generation
workflows ( Zhuge et al., 2025 ) . Agentic approaches
gather additional evidence by iteratively inspecting recorded
trajectories ( Wan et al., 2026 ) or interacting with the execution
environment ( Cui et al., 2026 ) . Evidence-first verification separates
investigation from validation, checking proposed claims against their
state or trace sources before accepting rubric
verdicts ( Sanayei et al., 2026 ) . These approaches motivate both
seeking task-relevant evidence and assessing how it supports a judgment.
VeriCUA builds its rubric after inspecting the available environment or
recording, then selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements.
Source-aware rules combine the resulting findings within a shared offline
and online verification workflow.

Each finding identifies a rubric requirement, states the support or

code-based checks of stored artifacts. Task-specific checkers can be
reused across repeated executions of the same task with compatible

tasks to avoid assigning training or filtering labels unsupported by the

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We presented VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verifying
computer-using agents through agentic exploration. The verifier inspects
available context before constructing a task rubric, then selects GUI or
code checks to gather evidence for unresolved requirements. Source-aware
arbitration combines the findings within a shared workflow for offline
recordings and online environments. Across the evaluated platforms, VeriCUA improves agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines, with
fewer false positives online and the largest offline gains on hard
trajectories. Analyses show that complementary evidence sources and
verification passes improve decision coverage, while stronger backbones
further improve accuracy. These results support agentic verification for
CUA evaluation and motivate its use in data curation and reinforcement
learning.

网上的假阳性反应减少 并且是最大的离线收益
轨相. 分析表明,补充证据来源和
核查证可扩大决策范围,而主干网则更强
进一步提高准确性。 这些成果支持代理核查

storage, against which requirements about a change are compared. The agent’s submitted answer is extracted by the
harness and exposed through the submitted_answer getter as the
artifact under test.

blocks.en: Appendix E Limitations and Broader Impacts
blocks.zh: 附录E 限制和更广泛的影响

blocks.en:
VeriCUA trades cost for evidence. A verification pass issues tens of tool calls
and model calls per trajectory, an order of magnitude more than a single-call
judge, so it suits filtering and reward assignment better than interactive
use. On recorded trajectories it abstains wherever the recording
holds no evidence for a requirement. Those abstentions are a coverage limit,
and online access lifts it only for environments that can be
instrumented. A stochastic verifier also needs its draw-to-draw spread reported beside every
comparison, as we do. Reliable trajectory verification lowers the cost of
training computer-using agents and of auditing benchmark labels. The same
machinery could be misused to certify agents that act on real systems, which
is one reason VeriCUA never writes to the environment it verifies.
